desc:
You stand at index 0 of nums. From index i one jump takes you to any index j with i < j ≤ i + nums[i], as long as j is inside the array. You may make at most k jumps (possibly none).

Return the largest index you can stand on after at most k jumps.

nums = [2, 3, 1, 1, 4], k = 1 -> 2
nums = [2, 3, 1, 1, 4], k = 2 -> 4   (0 -> 1 -> 4)
nums = [1, 0, 5], k = 9       -> 1   (stuck at index 1)
hints: After j jumps, the set of indices you can stand on is easy to describe. Is it a contiguous range?
Yes: after j jumps every index from 0 to some reach_j can be reached with at most j jumps (a jump may be shorter than allowed). So you only need to track one number.
reach_{j+1} = max(i + nums[i]) over all i ≤ reach_j, capped at n-1. Stop early when it no longer grows, so a huge k costs nothing; scan each index only once.
editorial: Let reach_j be the farthest index reachable with at most j jumps. Because a jump can be any length up to the maximum, everything between 0 and reach_j is reachable too, so the reachable set is the prefix [0, reach_j]. The next frontier is the best landing of any index in that prefix: reach_{j+1} = min(n-1, max(i + nums[i])) for i in the prefix.

Run this for at most k rounds. To keep it linear, remember how far the scan already got, so each index is looked at once overall. If a round does not extend the reach, nothing will ever change again and you can stop; this also bounds the number of rounds by n even when k is 10<sup>9</sup>.
This is the layered-BFS view of the Jump Game II greedy, but it asks for the farthest position instead of the number of jumps. Time O(n), space O(1).
